sections.title: 5.1 Discover
sections.summary: Raw cryptographic touchpoints from a sweep of the lab, and a second source that shows what one method misses.

blocks.markdown:
The first phase produces **raw evidence**: every cryptographic touchpoint that discovery can find, with the observations as made (protocol version, cipher suite, certificate subject, key type, signature algorithm), and nothing yet cleaned, merged or interpreted. Keeping the raw output matters because later phases will reorganise it and a reviewer must be able to go back to what was actually observed.

The listing sweeps ports 47100 to 47129 on 127.0.0.1 (this machine only), identifies each listener by a TLS handshake or a banner, and prints the raw rows. It then compares the result with a second, independent source of names (DEMO DATA, standing for DNS or certificate-transparency records) to show what a single method misses. Discovery, inventory, classification, ranking, prototype, monitoring and hybrid listings run against the same **local lab** as module E2 (TLS and plain services on 127.0.0.1, this machine only, ports 47100 upwards) or against real cryptographic code. Business inputs (owners, impact, lifetimes), waves, freeze windows, pilot failure rates and traffic logs are **DEMO DATA / SIMULATION**, labelled where used. Nothing here is a finding about a real organisation. The course divides the migration into twelve phases; the book's own prescriptive approach has five steps (discover, assess and prioritise, design a crypto-agile architecture, migrate, monitor), which the twelve phases expand.

blocks.markdown:
The sweep finds **six touchpoints**: five TLS services (web.lab.test with RSA-2048, billing.lab.test with RSA-1024, api.lab.test with ECDSA P-256, intra.lab.test with RSA-2048, edge.lab.test with Ed25519) and one plain service with an SSH-style banner. Against the second source, three published names (mail, portal and vpn) were **not reached** by the sweep (other hosts, other ports, or not reachable from here), and two services that the sweep found (edge and intra) are **not published**.

**Rules for the phase.** Use more than one source, record the method and time of every observation, keep the raw output as evidence, and do not interpret yet. The result is **not an inventory**: it has gaps (names without a reachable endpoint), surprises (endpoints without a name) and no owners. **Common mistake:** treating the first scan as the asset list and starting the migration from it.

sections.title: 5.2 Inventory
sections.summary: Normalising raw rows into validated records with owners from an asset register, keeping flawed records flagged instead of dropping them.

blocks.markdown:
The **inventory** turns raw rows into a structured, validated record per asset: a stable identifier, the endpoint, protocol, key-exchange class, authentication key type and size, signature algorithm, expiry bucket and an **owner**. Module E2.1 describes the CBOM format for it; this phase is the practice of building and maintaining it. Three rules govern it: records are **validated** against a schema (required fields, enumerations, value checks), records with problems are **kept and flagged** (never silently dropped, or the inventory would look healthier than the estate), and the inventory is **versioned** with the date of last observation.

The listing normalises the five lab TLS services into records, derives a key-exchange class from the cipher suite (for TLS 1.3 it states honestly that the key-exchange group was not read), joins the owner from an asset register (DEMO DATA, with one name missing from the register) and validates each record. Discovery, inventory, classification, ranking, prototype, monitoring and hybrid listings run against the same **local lab** as module E2 (TLS and plain services on 127.0.0.1, this machine only, ports 47100 upwards) or against real cryptographic code. Business inputs (owners, impact, lifetimes), waves, freeze windows, pilot failure rates and traffic logs are **DEMO DATA / SIMULATION**, labelled where used. import datetime, os, socket, ssl, tempfile, threading
from cryptography import x509
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes, serialization
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ec, ed25519, rsa
from cryptography.x509.oid import NameOID

# ---- lab: small TLS servers on 127.0.0.1 that this script starts and then discovers. Certificates are self-signed and generated now. ----
def make_cert(kind, cn, valid_from_days, valid_to_days):
    if kind == "rsa1024": key = rsa.generate_private_key(65537, 1024)
    elif kind == "rsa2048": key = rsa.generate_private_key(65537, 2048)
    elif kind == "ec256": key = ec.generate_private_key(ec.SECP256R1())
    elif kind == "ed25519": key = ed25519.Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()
    sign_hash = None if kind == "ed25519" else hashes.SHA256()
    name = x509.Name([x509.NameAttribute(NameOID.COMMON_NAME, cn)])
    now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)
    cert = (x509.CertificateBuilder().subject_name(name).issuer_name(name).public_key(key.public_key()).serial_number(x509.random_serial_number())
            .not_valid_before(now + datetime.timedelta(days=valid_from_days)).not_valid_after(now + datetime.timedelta(days=valid_to_days))
            .add_extension(x509.SubjectAlternativeName([x509.DNSName(cn)]), critical=False).sign(key, sign_hash))
    return key, cert

LAB = [  # label, key kind, common name, validity (from, to) in days relative to now, highest TLS version the server accepts
    ("web-front",      "rsa2048", "web.lab.test",     (-30, 335), ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_3),
    ("legacy-billing", "rsa1024", "billing.lab.test", (-900, 200), ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_2),
    ("api-gateway",    "ec256",   "api.lab.test",     (-10, 80),  ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_3),
    ("old-intranet",   "rsa2048", "intra.lab.test",   (-400, -35), ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_2),
    ("edge-device",    "ed25519", "edge.lab.test",    (-5, 3000), ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_3),
]
_tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
_next_port = [47100]
def bind_free():
    """bind the next free port from 47100 upwards on 127.0.0.1 (a fixed small range makes the discovery sweep below short and repeatable)"""
    while True:
        s = socket.socket()
        try:
            s.bind(("127.0.0.1", _next_port[0])); s.listen(16); _next_port[0] += 1
            return s
        except OSError:
            s.close(); _next_port[0] += 1
def start_lab():
    servers = {}
    for label, kind, cn, (a, b), maxv in LAB:
        key, cert = make_cert(kind, cn, a, b)
        cf, kf = os.path.join(_tmp, label + ".crt"), os.path.join(_tmp, label + ".key")
        open(cf, "wb").write(cert.public_bytes(serialization.Encoding.PEM))
        open(kf, "wb").write(key.private_bytes(serialization.Encoding.PEM, serialization.PrivateFormat.PKCS8, serialization.NoEncryption()))
        ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
        ctx.minimum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_2
        ctx.maximum_version = maxv
        ctx.set_ciphers("DEFAULT:@SECLEVEL=0")
        ctx.load_cert_chain(cf, kf)
        sock = bind_free()
        def serve(s=sock, c=ctx):
            while True:
                try:
                    conn, _ = s.accept()
                except OSError:
                    return
                try:
                    with c.wrap_socket(conn, server_side=True) as t:
                        t.settimeout(1)
                except Exception:
                    pass
        threading.Thread(target=serve, daemon=True).start()
        servers[label] = sock.getsockname()[1]
    return servers

def probe(port, minv=None, maxv=None):
    """TLS client handshake to 127.0.0.1:port; returns (version, cipher, DER certificate) or None if the server refuses"""
    ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)
    ctx.check_hostname = False; ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
    ctx.set_ciphers("DEFAULT:@SECLEVEL=0")
    ctx.minimum_version = minv or ssl.TLSVersion.MINIMUM_SUPPORTED
    if maxv: ctx.maximum_version = maxv
    try:
        with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port), timeout=3) as raw:
            with ctx.wrap_socket(raw) as t:
                return t.version(), t.cipher()[0], t.getpeercert(binary_form=True)
    except (ssl.SSLError, OSError):
        return None

def describe_key(cert):
    pk = cert.public_key()
    if isinstance(pk, rsa.RSAPublicKey): return "RSA", pk.key_size
    if isinstance(pk, ec.EllipticCurvePublicKey): return "EC " + pk.curve.name, pk.key_size
    if isinstance(pk, ed25519.Ed25519PublicKey): return "Ed25519", 256
    return type(pk).__name__, 0

def start_plain(payload):
    """a non-TLS service that sends 'payload' bytes to every client and closes (used for banner and SSH-style discovery)"""
    sock = bind_free()
    def serve():
        while True:
            try:
                conn, _ = sock.accept()
            except OSError:
                return
            try:
                conn.sendall(payload)
            except OSError:
                pass
            conn.close()
    threading.Thread(target=serve, daemon=True).start()
    return sock.getsockname()[1]
import json
# Phase 2, Inventory: normalise raw discovery into a validated record per asset, attach an owner from the asset register (DEMO DATA) and report invalid or unowned records.
servers = start_lab()
OWNERS = {"web.lab.test": "web team", "billing.lab.test": "finance IT", "api.lab.test": "platform", "intra.lab.test": None}      # edge.lab.test is not registered
def kex_class(version, cipher):
    if version == "TLSv1.3": return "TLS 1.3: key-exchange group not read"
    return "ECDHE" if cipher.startswith("ECDHE") else "DHE" if cipher.startswith("DHE") else "RSA key transport"
today = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)
records = []
for label, port in servers.items():
    version, cipher, der = probe(port)
    c = x509.load_der_x509_certificate(der)
    alg, size = describe_key(c)
    left = (c.not_valid_after_utc - today).days
    cn = c.subject.get_attributes_for_oid(NameOID.COMMON_NAME)[0].value
    records.append({"asset": label, "name": cn, "protocol": version, "kex": kex_class(version, cipher), "cipher": cipher, "auth_key": alg, "key_bits": size,
                    "signature": c.signature_algorithm_oid._name, "expiry": "EXPIRED" if left < 0 else "within 90 days" if left <= 90 else "later", "owner": OWNERS.get(cn)})
REQUIRED = ("asset", "name", "protocol", "kex", "auth_key", "key_bits", "signature", "expiry")
def validate(r):
    problems = [f"missing {f}" for f in REQUIRED if r.get(f) in (None, "")]
    if r["auth_key"] == "RSA" and r["key_bits"] < 2048: problems.append("RSA key below 2048 bits")
    if r["owner"] is None: problems.append("no owner in the asset register")
    return problems
print(f"{'asset':<16} {'protocol':<9} {'key exchange':<38} {'auth key':<14} {'expiry':<15} {'owner':<11} problems")
for r in records:
    p = validate(r)
    print(f"{r['asset']:<16} {r['protocol']:<9} {r['kex']:<38} {r['auth_key'] + ' ' + str(r['key_bits']):<14} {r['expiry']:<15} {str(r['owner']):<11} {'; '.join(p) or '-'}")
print()
ok = [r for r in records if not validate(r)]
print(f"{len(records)} records, {len(ok)} valid and owned, {len(records) - len(ok)} need action before they can enter the inventory of record")
print("record as stored (JSON):")
print(json.dumps(records[0], indent=1))
print("rule: a record with problems is KEPT and flagged, never dropped; the inventory of record is versioned, and each record keeps the date of its last observation")

blocks.markdown:
Of the five records, **two are valid and owned**; three need action: the legacy-billing record has an **RSA key below 2048 bits**, and old-intranet and edge-device have **no owner in the asset register** (old-intranet's certificate has also **expired**, which the table shows in its expiry column). The key-exchange column shows `ECDHE` for the two TLS 1.2 services and *key-exchange group not read* for the three TLS 1.3 services, which is the honest statement: the group would tell classical X25519 from a hybrid and this probe cannot read it. The stored form is a JSON record.

**Why "kept and flagged".** If invalid records were dropped, the inventory would show only the healthy part of the estate and the migration would start from a biased list. Flagged records become tasks: assign an owner, replace the weak key, find out what the service carries. **Common mistake:** requiring complete records before admitting an asset, which hides exactly the assets that need attention.

options: It is kept and flagged for action

blocks.question: Why does the key-exchange column say the group was not read for TLS 1.3?
options: The probe cannot see the group, and the record must not claim more than was observed
blocks.explanation: Reading the group needs a raw handshake probe.

options: Someone must be accountable for each asset's migration

sections.title: 5.3 Classify
sections.summary: Explicit tiering rules over business function, impact and secrecy lifetime, with unclassified assets sent back to owners instead of receiving a default.

blocks.markdown:
**Classification** attaches business meaning to the inventory: which **function** an asset serves, the **impact** of a confidentiality loss and the **secrecy lifetime** of the data (E1.3), and from them a **tier** that sets the migration priority. The rules must be written down so that the classification is reproducible. The two inputs are independent axes: high impact with a short lifetime and low impact with a long lifetime can both land in the top tier, for different reasons.

The listing classifies the five lab assets from an invented business mapping (DEMO DATA) with the rules *tier 1 = high impact or secrecy lifetime of 20 years or more; tier 2 = moderate impact or 5 years or more; otherwise tier 3; no mapping = unclassified*. sections.title: 5.5 Select PQC
sections.summary: A written decision procedure from requirements to ML-KEM, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA with the reason printed, the size trade-offs, and the status of HQC.

blocks.markdown:
Selecting algorithms is a **decision with stated reasons**. For **key establishment** the standardised choice is ML-KEM (FIPS 203) in the parameter set that matches the security category (ML-KEM-768 is the common default, ML-KEM-1024 for 256-bit policies), combined with a classical component during the transition (5.9). For **signatures** the general-purpose standard is ML-DSA (FIPS 204: ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87), and for signatures that must stay valid for decades or that should not rest on a lattice assumption, **SLH-DSA** (FIPS 205) rests only on hash-function security at the price of much larger signatures (7,856 bytes for the small SHA2-128s set).

The listing encodes the procedure as code with the reason printed for each choice and applies it to five requirements, including a signature budget of 128 bytes for a meter and a 15-year firmware root. The sizes printed are those of the standards. Discovery, inventory, classification, ranking, prototype, monitoring and hybrid listings run against the same **local lab** as module E2 (TLS and plain services on 127.0.0.1, this machine only, ports 47100 upwards) or against real cryptographic code. Business inputs (owners, impact, lifetimes), waves, freeze windows, pilot failure rates and traffic logs are **DEMO DATA / SIMULATION**, labelled where used. Nothing here is a finding about a real organisation.

from dataclasses import dataclass
# Phase 5, Select PQC: a written decision procedure from requirements to algorithm, with the reason printed for each choice. Sizes are bytes from the NIST standards (FIPS 203, 204, 205).
SIZES = {"ML-KEM-768": "public key 1184, ciphertext 1088", "ML-KEM-1024": "public key 1568, ciphertext 1568", "ML-DSA-44": "public key 1312, signature 2420",
         "ML-DSA-65": "public key 1952, signature 3309", "ML-DSA-87": "public key 2592, signature 4627", "SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s": "public key 32, signature 7856", "SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f": "public key 32, signature 17088"}
@dataclass
class Need:
    name: str
    purpose: str                 # "key establishment" or "signature"
    strength: int = 128          # classical-equivalent security strength wanted: 128, 192 or 256
    sig_budget: int = 10 ** 9    # largest tolerable signature in bytes
    verify_only_device: bool = False
    long_lived_root: bool = False  # signatures that must stay valid for decades (firmware roots, CA roots)
    must_be_hybrid: bool = True
def select(n):
    why = []
    if n.purpose == "key establishment":
        alg = "ML-KEM-1024" if n.strength >= 256 else "ML-KEM-768"
        why.append("FIPS 203 is the standardised KEM; " + ("category 5 for 256-bit strength" if alg.endswith("1024") else "category 3 is the common default"))
        if n.must_be_hybrid:
            alg = "X25519+" + alg; why.append("combined with X25519 during the transition: secure if either component holds (E5.9)")
        return alg, why
    if n.long_lived_root:
        why.append("a long-lived root should not depend on one mathematical assumption: SLH-DSA (hash-based, FIPS 205) rests only on hash security")
        alg = "SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s" if n.sig_budget >= 7856 else None
        if alg is None: why.append(f"BUT the signature budget of {n.sig_budget} bytes is below 7856: no SLH-DSA parameter set fits; use ML-DSA with a short-lived key chain or revise the format")
        return alg or "ML-DSA-65 (budget forces the trade-off)", why
    order = [("ML-DSA-44", 2420), ("ML-DSA-65", 3309), ("ML-DSA-87", 4627)]
    want = {128: "ML-DSA-44", 192: "ML-DSA-65", 256: "ML-DSA-87"}[n.strength]
    sig = dict(order)[want]
    why.append("FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) is the general-purpose standardised signature")
    if sig > n.sig_budget: why.append(f"BUT its signature of {sig} bytes exceeds the budget of {n.sig_budget}: the format must change first (E4.8)")
    return want, why

    Need("backup key wrapping, 256-bit policy", "key establishment", strength=256),
    Need("internal service signatures", "signature", strength=192),
    Need("firmware signing root, 15-year device life", "signature", long_lived_root=True, sig_budget=16384),
    Need("meter firmware, 128-byte header field", "signature", long_lived_root=True, sig_budget=128),
]
for n in needs:
    alg, why = select(n)
    print(f"== {n.name}\n   choice: {alg}")
    for w in why: print("   -", w)

sections.title: 5.6 Prototype
sections.summary: A loopback client and server that exchange KEM public keys and ciphertexts and then protected data, used to find size, framing and failure-behaviour surprises early.

blocks.markdown:
A **prototype** is a small, controlled implementation that answers integration questions before any production commitment: do the larger messages fit the protocol fields and buffers, how does failure show up, what must both ends agree on beforehand. It applies the implementation practices of module C9 (constant-time primitives from a maintained library, no custom crypto) to a toy protocol.

The listing builds a **client and server over loopback TCP** using the KEM layer of E4.1: the server sends its public key, the client answers with a ciphertext, both derive an AES-256-GCM key and the client sends one protected message. It runs this for X25519, ECDH-P256, ML-KEM-768 and the hybrid, prints the sizes of each flight and the number of TCP segments they need at an MSS of 1460 bytes, and demonstrates how a corrupted ML-KEM ciphertext behaves. Discovery, inventory, classification, ranking, prototype, monitoring and hybrid listings run against the same **local lab** as module E2 (TLS and plain services on 127.0.0.1, this machine only, ports 47100 upwards) or against real cryptographic code. Business inputs (owners, impact, lifetimes), waves, freeze windows, pilot failure rates and traffic logs are **DEMO DATA / SIMULATION**, labelled where used. Nothing here is a finding about a real organisation.

sections.title: 5.8 Pilot
sections.summary: A simulated staged rollout with a statistical stop gate: a clear regression is stopped at the 1 percent canary, a small regression is not, and why the gate's tolerance defines what it can see.

blocks.markdown:
A **pilot** deploys the benchmarked change to a limited, monitored part of production. import math, random
# Phase 8, Pilot: a staged rollout with a statistical gate at every stage. SIMULATION: the true failure rates are ASSUMED values chosen to show the logic; this is not data from any real pilot.
def wilson(failures, n, z=1.96):
    p = failures / n
    centre = p + z * z / (2 * n)
    margin = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n))
    return (centre - margin) / (1 + z * z / n), (centre + margin) / (1 + z * z / n)

TOLERANCE = 0.002           # the gate stops the pilot only when the data show, with 95% confidence, a failure rate above baseline + tolerance
LIMIT = BASELINE + TOLERANCE
STAGES = [("canary 1%", 0.01), ("5%", 0.05), ("25%", 0.25), ("100%", 1.0)]
DAILY = 200_000

sections.title: 5.9 Hybrid Migration
sections.summary: The hybrid property shown directly: an attacker who breaks one component and guesses the other cannot derive the key, ciphertexts are bound into the key, and the four migration states with their costs.

blocks.markdown:
For most organisations the production path runs through **hybrid cryptography**: a classical and a post-quantum algorithm used together, with a combiner that makes the final key depend on both. The security argument is simple: the session key is safe if **either** component holds, so a flaw found in the new post-quantum algorithm does not undo today's protection, and the quantum break of the classical one does not expose the session.

The listing takes the hybrid KEM of E4.1 apart and checks the argument directly: the receiver derives the key from both component secrets and both ciphertexts; an attacker is then given one component secret (as if that component were broken) and has to guess the other; and a ciphertext is swapped to show that the ciphertexts are bound into the key. It ends with the four migration states of a service (classical only, hybrid with classical accepted, hybrid required, post-quantum only). The combiner is **illustrative**; deployments use the construction in the standard they adopt (for example the hybrid TLS 1.3 key-exchange specification). Discovery, inventory, classification, ranking, prototype, monitoring and hybrid listings run against the same **local lab** as module E2 (TLS and plain services on 127.0.0.1, this machine only, ports 47100 upwards) or against real cryptographic code. Business inputs (owners, impact, lifetimes), waves, freeze windows, pilot failure rates and traffic logs are **DEMO DATA / SIMULATION**, labelled where used. Nothing here is a finding about a real organisation.

The last phase is the one most often delayed: **retiring** the classical-only fallback. Until it is switched off, an attacker who can force a downgrade (or a client that never upgrades) keeps the old exposure alive.
